title: Not punishment
hookLine: Job's friends were wrong: suffering isn't proof you've failed

cards: Some people arrive with terrible news. Pilate has killed a group of Galileans while they were offering their sacrifices. Their blood is mixed with the blood of the animals.
In Luke's Gospel, the people tell this to Jesus, and a question hangs in the air that nobody says out loud.

He says it for them: "Suppose ye that these Galilaeans were sinners above all the Galilaeans, because they suffered such things?" It's an old question, and it comes up after a diagnosis, a layoff, a crash.
What did they do to deserve it? What did I?

teach.b: First, the old equation. Suffer, and you must have done something. It's the logic of Job's friends.
Eliphaz asks Job to name one innocent person who ever perished, as if the answer settled things. At the end of the book, God tells the friends they have not spoken rightly, as Job has.
The book of Job doesn't explain suffering. But it does refuse the equation. Second, the answer in Luke.
Jesus answers his own question: "I tell you, Nay."

Then he raises a second disaster, one with no villain at all: "those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem?"
Third, the hard line after it. Jesus goes on: "except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish." Readers take that in different ways.

Some hear it as a call to everyone listening to turn to God, because life is short and nobody is safe. Others hear a warning about the coming troubles of that time. What it doesn't do is say the eighteen earned the tower.
Fourth, time and chance. Ecclesiastes, a book of the Hebrew Bible, puts it plainly: "time and chance happeneth to them all." Towers fall.
Cells divide wrong. Companies close. Some suffering has causes we can name and change, and that's worth knowing.
But in these texts, a hard thing landing on someone is not, by itself, a verdict on that someone. That holds for the people on the news, and it holds closer to home.

how: Jewish and Christian readers turn to the book of Job, Luke 13:1–5 and Ecclesiastes 9:11 when someone asks whether a disaster was deserved, and some pastoral counselors use these texts to gently challenge the idea that suffering is proof of guilt.

o: a hard thing is fine as long as you don't complain
suffering isn't, by itself, proof that someone failed
pain is always a sign you made a wrong choice

games.q: people tell Jesus that Pilate has killed some Galileans at their sacrifices. the unspoken question: were they worse sinners? what does he say?
o: yes, it must have been deserved.
games.why: "I tell you, nay." then he adds the eighteen under the tower of Siloam, and answers the same way.

practice: Is there something hard in your life you've quietly filed under my fault, or what I deserve? Not a real mistake you might want to make right, but a story that says the suffering itself proves something bad about you.
Hold it lightly, then on an out-breath set it down like a heavy bag at the door, and breathe without it; if you pray, you can hand it to God.
